hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up on $\frac{\sec^2\theta - 1}{\tan^2\theta}$: the numerator IS $\tan^2\theta$, so the whole thing is $1$. Replacing $\sec^2\theta - 1$ first is the opening move in your problem too.

explanation: The $\sin^2\theta$ terms cancel, leaving $\frac{1}{\cos^2\theta}$, which is $\sec^2\theta$.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The tempting wrong answer is $\tan^2\theta$ (choice B): students correctly rewrite the numerator as $\tan^2\theta$ and then stop, forgetting the denominator is still sitting there.
Simplifying is not finished until every piece has been used — you still have to divide by $\sin^2\theta$.
The habit that saves you: convert everything to sines and cosines, then cancel. That never lets you leave a factor behind. The answer is $\sec^2\theta$.
